summary: Describes the architecture of Segment Routing (SR) policies. An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments, which are instructions, that steers packet flows along a chosen path using source routing. Packets are steered into a policy at a headend node, so intermediate routers do not need per-path state. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Instead of each crossroad deciding, the first router writes a list of stops on the package, like a travel itinerary. Each stop follows the list, so the roads need not remember anything.

questions: how does segment routing steer traffic
how does an sr policy pick its active candidate path
what is the color in an sr policy
what is drop upon invalid in segment routing
subtitle: How a router holds an ordered list of segments as a named policy and steers traffic into it.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing lets a node steer a flow along any path, but the pieces needed to define, select, validate and use such a path as a policy were not specified in detail.
tldr.mechanism: An SR Policy is identified by headend, color and endpoint and holds candidate paths made of segment lists. The headend picks one active path by preference and steers traffic into it, for example by matching a BGP color or a Binding SID.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9256 is a Standards Track specification that updates RFC 8402. It applies equally to SR-MPLS and SRv6 and defines no new protocol extensions.

today: RFC 9256 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track) from July 2022 that updates RFC 8402, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It works with the SR-MPLS and SRv6 data plane documents, RFC 8660, RFC 8754 and RFC 8986.

sections.title: Segment Routing and Policies
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) lets a node steer a packet flow along any path. The headend is the node that writes the instructions, called segments, into the packet, so intermediate routers keep no per-path state. An SR Policy is an ordered list of segments that represents a source-routed policy, and the headend is said to steer a flow into it.

RFC 8660 describes the segment list as an MPLS label stack for SR-MPLS. RFC 8754 and RFC 8986 describe it for Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6), using the Segment Routing Header. RFC 9256 updates RFC 8402 with the detailed concepts of SR Policy and of steering into one, and applies equally to both data planes.
sections.eli5: The first router writes a list of stops on your package. Every router after that just follows the list and does not need to remember anything.

sections.title: Identity and Candidate Paths
sections.content:
An SR Policy MUST be identified by the tuple <Headend, Color, Endpoint>. The headend is an IPv4 or IPv6 address that MUST resolve to a unique node. The endpoint is the destination, also an address. The color is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit integer that ties the policy to an intent, such as low latency. Endpoint and color together automate the steering of service and transport routes onto policies. An implementation MAY also give a policy a symbolic name for debugging.

A policy has one or more candidate paths, the unit of signaling to a headend, for example through PCEP or BGP. Each holds segment lists, and a candidate path is one of three kinds:

  • Explicit: given as a segment list or a set of them. The headend does not compute it, it only checks validity.
  • Dynamic: given as an optimization objective plus constraints. The headend, possibly with help from a PCE, computes the segment list.
  • Composite: a container that groups other SR Policies for load-balanced steering. The constituents MUST have the same endpoint as the parent, MUST each have a color different from the parent's, and MUST NOT themselves use composite paths.

When a candidate path has several segment lists, each carries a weight (default 1), and flows are spread by weighted ECMP in proportion w/Sw. A candidate path is identified by <Protocol-Origin, Originator, Discriminator>, never by its segment list. Symbolic names MUST NOT be treated as identifiers.
sections.eli5: A policy is like a travel plan with a name tag: where it starts, where it ends, and what it is for. It can hold several route options, and some options can split the traffic by weight.

sections.title: Choosing the Active Candidate Path
sections.content:
A candidate path is usable when valid. The one used for forwarding is the active path: the valid one with the highest Preference, a 32-bit value whose default is 100. The selection process MUST be rerun whenever a path is learned, deleted, changed or its validity changes. It is RECOMMENDED that each candidate path of a policy has a different Preference.

Ties in Preference are broken in this order:

  1. The higher Protocol-Origin wins.
  2. If configured, prefer the existing installed path.
  3. The lower Originator wins.
  4. The higher Discriminator wins.

The Originator is a 160-bit value made of an ASN and a node address, so redundant controllers give a deterministic outcome. The Discriminator is a 32-bit value that makes the final choice independent of the order in which paths arrive. A policy is valid when it has at least one valid candidate path.
sections.eli5: Each route option has a score. The highest score that is still working wins, and if two tie, a fixed list of tie-break rules picks one so every router makes the same choice.

sections.title: Segment Types
sections.content:
A segment list is an ordered set <S1, S2, ... Sn>. Whatever the data plane, the list can be written with different segment-descriptor types, lettered A to K. Types A and B give a ready MPLS label or SRv6 SID. Types C to K name something the headend must resolve: an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix with an optional SR algorithm, or an adjacency identified by an interface ID or by a pair of local and remote link addresses. For types C to K a SID value MAY also be supplied so the headend can verify it.

When no algorithm is given, the headend SHOULD use the Strict Shortest Path algorithm if available, otherwise the default Shortest Path algorithm. The first segment is the topmost MPLS label or the first SRv6 SID. For example, with segment list <16002, 16003, 16004, 2> the trailing label 2 is the IPv6 Explicit NULL label, which lets IPv6 traffic ride a path built from IPv4 Prefix SIDs. When steering unlabeled IPv6 BGP traffic and no such label is the bottom label, the headend SHOULD impose one.
sections.eli5: You can write a stop on the list as an exact street number, or as a name that the first router looks up for you. Both end up as the same kind of instruction on the package.

sections.title: Validity and Binding SIDs
sections.content:
An explicit segment list is invalid if it is empty, has weight 0, mixes SR-MPLS and SRv6 types, or if the headend cannot resolve the first SID to an outgoing interface and next hop, cannot resolve a later type C to K SID, or fails a verification it was asked to do. An explicit path is invalid once it has no valid segment list. A dynamic path is invalid if no solution meets its objective and constraints. A composite path is valid when at least one constituent policy is valid.

The Binding SID (BSID) provides scaling, network opacity and service independence. A candidate path MAY have one, candidate paths of one policy SHOULD share it, and paths of different policies MUST NOT. The BSID of a policy is that of its active path, if the value is available. If it is not, an alert MUST be generated, for example through syslog, and the policy MAY bind another one dynamically. Because the BSID can change when the active path changes, it SHOULD NOT be used to identify a policy. With the optional Specified-BSID-only behavior, a path whose BSID is unspecified or unavailable is invalid.

A valid policy installs a BSID-keyed forwarding entry that steers matching packets onto the selected path.
sections.eli5: A route option only counts if every stop on it makes sense. The binding SID is a shortcut ticket: show it, and the whole trip list is attached for you.

sections.title: Steering Traffic into a Policy
sections.content:
A headend can steer into a valid policy in four ways: the incoming packet's active SID matches a local BSID, a BGP or service route recurses on the policy (per-destination), packets are sorted into a forwarding array of paths (per-flow), or a local routing policy overrides other paths.

For the BGP case, the headend learns a route R/r with next hop N and a Color Extended community C, has a valid policy for color C and endpoint N, and has a BGP policy that allows C to be used as SLA steering information. It then installs R/r with the policy as next hop instead of N. Any SID tied to the route, such as the VPN label V, is inserted after the segment list, as in <S1, S2, S3, V>. With several colors, the highest numerical color with a valid policy wins. If an operator authorizes it, BGP can also trigger a dynamic candidate path on demand.

By default, when a policy turns invalid it and its BSID leave the forwarding plane and traffic follows the classic forwarding table. With Drop-Upon-Invalid, the policy stays with a drop action so traffic is discarded instead of taking the IGP shortest path. For per-flow steering, the RFC's example uses an array indexed by forwarding class, with values 0 to 7 when derived from the MPLS TC bits; entry 0 is the IGP path.

Color-only steering offers alternatives when no policy matches the exact endpoint: Type 0 falls back to the IGP path, while Types 1 and 2 also try policies with a null endpoint, which is 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and :: for IPv6.
sections.eli5: The first router can choose a path by the label on the package, by where it is going, by what kind of traffic it is, or by a rule set by the owner. Color tags say what kind of trip the sender wants.

sections.title: State, Failures and Management
sections.content:
The headend keeps SR Policy state that MUST show whether the policy is in the forwarding plane, which candidate paths and segment lists are active, and why any are not, such as validation errors. It can be reported through BGP-LS or PCEP, and a YANG model is referenced for configuration and operation.

For failure recovery, an SR Policy built from TI-LFA protected IGP segments gets that protection, which the RFC describes as a 50 msec local technique. An SR Policy can also protect a link, as with segment list <3, 9, 6> on node 2 as a backup for link 2-to-6. A lower-preference candidate path MAY be set as backup, and fast reroute MAY then switch over in under 50 msec, with mechanisms like BFD for fast detection.
sections.eli5: If a road is closed, the router can already have a spare route ready and switch to it very fast, and it keeps notes about which route it is using and why.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8402, RFC 8660, RFC 8754 and RFC 8986 apply. The RFC adds that if an endpoint address is advertised by more than one node, through misconfiguration or spoofing, steered traffic may be diverted to an undesired node. A wrong Color Extended community on a BGP route can likewise send packets along undesired paths.

Symbolic names are free text from external parties, so there is no assurance they are accurate, and users should verify using the actual identifiers. The document defines no new protocol extensions and introduces no further security considerations. IANA created a Segment Types subregistry, with identifiers A to K in the initial registrations, under the Specification Required policy.
sections.eli5: If two routers claim the same address, or a color tag is wrong, traffic can end up in the wrong place. Names are just labels, so do not trust them without checking.
